summary:
Allwork.Space reports on JLL research showing European and global office attendance rising while workplace quality lags behind, particularly for focused work.

Attendance trends: global office attendance rose to an average of 3.2 days per week, up from 2.7 in 2024. The share of employees who believe the office enables productive work rose to 73% from 70%. Socializing (63%) and internal meetings (55%) are the main drivers of coming in, yet once onsite employees spend roughly 70% of their time on individual work and virtual calls, creating a mismatch between why people come in and what the space must support. Perceived effectiveness of offices for focused work fell from 66% to 64%. Commute time (48%) and cost (29%) remain the leading barriers to attendance.

Noise and acoustics: EMEA recorded the lowest Human Experience score of the measured regions at 88. Acoustics and sound privacy were the two lowest-performing workplace factors in the 2025 research. Employees also flagged problems with meeting rooms and equipment, with meeting rooms ranking seventh among the weakest factors.

Room demand: the share of required space allocated to rooms for two to four people rose from 39% to 43%, indicating growing demand for smaller meeting rooms. Meeting-room availability is further squeezed when employees occupy rooms for solo work and calls rather than collaboration.

Implications: rising attendance alone does not improve workplace experience. Employers are advised to focus on acoustics, private and quiet areas, meeting-room capacity, technology and amenities so that offices support collaboration, virtual meetings and concentrated individual work. Workplace quality is framed as central to whether employees see the commute as worthwhile.
